description_full: Brunello Cucinelli S.p.A., together with its subsidiaries, engages in the production and sale of clothing, accessories, and lifestyle products in Italy, Europe, the United States, and Asia. The company offers women's collection, including coats and jackets, blazers, knitwear, jumpsuits, dresses, t-shirts and tops, shirts, skirts, pants, denim, beach and travel wear, and matching sets; sneakers, heels, boots, loafers, sandals, and flat shoes; hats, belts, eyewear, jewelry, scarves, leather goods, and other accessories; mini bags and clutches; crossbody bags and backpacks; and handbags and shoppers. It also provides men's collection, such as coats and jackets, knitwear, blazers, suits, tuxedos, t-shirts and polos, shirts, pants, denim, travel and beach wear, and ready-to-wear products; sneakers, lace-ups, loafers, slides and flip-flops, espadrilles, leisure products, and other shoes; leather goods, bags, hats, belts, scarves; other accessories; and kids, fragrance, and gift products. In addition, the company offers lifestyle products, which include throws and blankets, cushions, studio products, candles and fragrances, travel essentials, décor sets, bathrobes and towels, leisure wear, kitchen and tableware, and dining and ceramic creation products. It sells its products through directly operated stores, hard shops, single-brand stores, independent multi-brand points of sale, and dedicated shop-in-shops in department stores, as well as online under the Brunello Cucinelli brand. Brunello Cucinelli S.p.A. was founded in 1978 and is headquartered in Solomeo, Italy. Brunello Cucinelli S.p.A. is a subsidiary of Fedone S.R.L.

financial_summary: BRUNELLO CUCINELLI is a mid-cap consumer cyclical business with a $6.9B market cap on $1.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +18% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.

Returns on capital run at 14% against a 7% cost of capital, a 7-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it. Gross margins of 91% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $111M in free cash flow — roughly 7 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.80× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.3× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 6.0×.

Shareholder yield is only 1.2%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 50% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 2.2× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 17% operating margin runs 10pp above the Consumer Cyclical median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.17x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 6% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range.
With annualised volatility of 6% and a beta of 0.51, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.17 vs 5y 0.31), so read it loosely.
In past sell-offs it fell 35% in the 2020 crash and 39% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $42.30 (margin of safety -140%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 10%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $27.24 to $65.07 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 45.4 vs 18.8, EV/EBITDA 24.8 vs 10.7 and P/FCF 62.1 vs 16.7 (sector median).
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 1.6% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 14.9% annual cash-flow growth, 11pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 14% earns above the cost of capital of 7.0%, but the 7pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have been steady (CV 0.14).
It runs a 91% gross margin and converts 7% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.80x.
ROE of 25% is amplified by 3.7x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.3x net debt to EBITDA ($224.8M of cash against $1.3B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 6.0x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.9, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 18.0% over 3 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 7% of profits supports about 1.0% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
own: Insiders own 50.0%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 30%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.2% (0.1% in buybacks and 1.2% in dividends).
people: With about 3,542 employees, each generates about $438K of revenue, in line with the Consumer Cyclical median.
That works out to $31K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.9M (4x revenue per employee).
